topics.title: Folk wisdom tales, morals and proverbs

learn.hook: Two brothers, one big basket of mangoes and a fight that could last forever. Can one wise sentence fix it?
points: The lesson 'Wisdom Paves the Way' is a folk story in which clear, wise thinking opens a way out of a difficult problem.

Folk tales are stories passed down by word of mouth over many generations, so their first authors are usually unknown. India has a rich storytelling tradition, including folk tales and well-loved fable collections like the Panchatantra.
Folk tales often have a simple setting, a problem, a wise or clever character, and a moral, which is the lesson the story teaches.
A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice: 'Look before you leap', 'A stitch in time saves nine', 'Two heads are better than one'.
'Wisdom' is a noun. Its adjective is 'wise' and its adverb is 'wisely'.

example.q: Read this original tale: Two brothers in a Rajasthan village quarrelled over a basket of mangoes left by their grandfather. Each said the other would cheat. Old Gomti-ma listened and said, "Let one of you divide the mangoes into two heaps, and let the other choose first." The quarrel ended at once. Think it through: why does her plan make the sharing fair?
steps: One brother divides; the other picks first.
If the divider makes one heap smaller, the other brother will take the bigger heap.
So the divider is forced to make the two heaps as equal as he can.
Neither brother can complain: one made the heaps, the other chose.
example.answer: The divider must make equal heaps, because any bigger heap would be chosen by the other brother.

learn.reallife: When two friends share a samosa, one cuts and the other chooses. You are using Gomti-ma's wisdom!

games.title: Proverb and meaning
pairs: A stitch in time saves nine
Two heads are better than one
Where there's a will, there's a way
Slow and steady wins the race

games.title: Folk tales: true or false?
items: Folk tales were usually passed down by word of mouth.
People told them aloud to the next generation long before they were written down.
A moral is the lesson that a story teaches.
The moral is the message or lesson we take away.
A proverb is a long story with many characters.
A proverb is a short, well-known saying, not a story.
In Gomti-ma's plan, the same brother both divides and chooses.
One brother divides and the other chooses first. That is what makes it fair.
The Panchatantra is a well-known collection of Indian animal fables.
Its stories use animals to teach lessons about wise living.

quiz.q: Read: Gomti-ma said, "Let one of you divide the mangoes into two heaps, and let the other choose first." Why will the divider make the heaps equal?
options: If one heap is smaller, the other brother will leave it for him
quiz.explain: The other brother chooses first and will take the bigger heap, so the divider gains nothing by being unfair.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about what the other brother will do

quiz.q: What does the phrase 'paves the way' mean in 'Wisdom paves the way'?
quiz.explain: To pave the way is to prepare a path so something can happen. Wisdom makes a solution possible.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'pave' only in its literal sense of laying a road

quiz.q: What is the adjective form of 'wisdom'?
quiz.explain: 'Wise' describes a person, so it is the adjective. 'Wisely' is the adverb.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the adjective with the adverb

quiz.q: Which of these is a proverb?
quiz.explain: 'Look before you leap' is a short traditional saying that gives advice: think before you act.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any short sentence is a proverb

quiz.q: Folk tales were mostly passed on ___.
quiz.explain: Folk tales come from times before printing, when people told stories aloud.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that folk tales are older than modern media

quiz.q: Which proverb fits? Meena got a small leak in the roof fixed before the monsoon, so the room stayed dry all season.
options: A stitch in time saves nine
Too many cooks spoil the broth
All that glitters is not gold
Slow and steady wins the race
quiz.explain: Fixing a small problem early stopped a bigger one later. That is what 'a stitch in time saves nine' means.
quiz.mistake: Picks a familiar proverb without matching its meaning

quiz.q: What do we call the lesson that a story teaches?
quiz.explain: The moral is the lesson. The setting is the time and place of the story.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the moral with the setting

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'wise'?
quiz.explain: A wise person and a sensible person both show good judgement. The other words mean the opposite.
quiz.mistake: Chooses an antonym instead of a synonym

teach.ask: Gappu asks: What is a folk tale, and what is the moral in a story like Gomti-ma's?
teach.praise: Hoot hoot! A folk tale is an old story passed down by telling, and its moral is the wise lesson inside it.
teach.nudge: How did folk tales travel before books? And what do we call the lesson a story gives?

topics.title: Problem solving: steps and linking words

learn.hook: A wise person does not panic. She goes step by step. And when we explain steps, little linking words do a big job!
points: Problem solving has clear steps: understand the problem, think of possible solutions, choose the best one, try it out, and check whether it worked.
Sequence connectors show the order of steps: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Cause and effect connectors join a reason and a result: because, as, so, therefore, as a result. 'Because' introduces the reason; 'so' introduces the result.
Contrast connectors show a difference or surprise: but, however, although, though.

example.q: Think it through: The plants in Class 8's garden dry up every summer holiday. Explain how to solve this using connectors.
steps: First, understand the problem: no one waters the plants during the holidays.
Next, list solutions: a watering rota, a drip bottle, or moving pots to shade.
Then, choose the best one: a rota of students who live nearby, because it is simple and free.
Finally, check after the holidays whether the plants survived.
example.answer: First understand, next list ideas, then choose and try the best one, and finally check the result.

learn.reallife: Recipes, science experiments and instructions for a board game all use sequence words like first, then and finally.

games.title: Steps to solve a problem
games.prompt: Put the problem-solving steps in order

items.text: The road was flooded, ___ we took the longer route.
We stayed indoors ___ it was raining heavily.
The plan was clever; ___, it needed more time.
___ the path was steep, the children kept climbing.

quiz.q: Which word shows the LAST step in a sequence?
quiz.explain: 'Finally' tells the reader that this is the last step.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'then' marks the end

quiz.q: Choose the connector: The well was dry, ___ the villagers dug a new one.
quiz.explain: The dry well is the reason; digging a new one is the result. 'So' introduces a result.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'because', which introduces a reason, not a result

quiz.q: Which sentence shows cause and effect?
options: It rained heavily, so the match was called off.
Rani is tall but her brother is short.
quiz.explain: Heavy rain (cause) led to the match being called off (effect), joined by 'so'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses contrast ('but') with cause and effect

quiz.q: What should you do FIRST when solving a problem?
quiz.explain: You cannot choose a good solution until you understand the problem.
quiz.mistake: Rushes to a solution before understanding the problem

quiz.q: 'Although the path was steep, the children kept climbing.' The word 'although' shows ___.
quiz.explain: 'Although' shows something surprising: the path was hard, yet they kept going.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'although' shows a reason

quiz.q: Pick the best order: (a) Water the seed (b) Dig a small hole (c) Put the seed in (d) Cover it with soil
quiz.explain: You dig the hole, place the seed, cover it with soil and then water it.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the order in which the steps are listed instead of the logical order

quiz.q: In a sentence, the connector 'because' introduces ___.
quiz.explain: 'Because' answers 'why?': We stayed in because it rained.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'because' (reason) with 'so' (result)

quiz.q: Choose the best connector: 'Ravi missed the bus. ___, he was late for school.'
quiz.explain: Being late is the result of missing the bus, so 'As a result' fits.
quiz.mistake: Puts 'because' before the result instead of before the reason

teach.ask: Gappu is stuck: My nest keeps falling apart! How should I solve this problem, and which words help me explain the steps?
teach.praise: First understand, then try ideas, finally check. And words like 'first', 'then' and 'finally' show the order. My nest will be strong!
teach.nudge: What is the very first step? Which little words show the order of steps? And what do you do at the end?

learn.hook: 'Give up', 'give in', 'give away': change one little word and the meaning flips! Meet phrasal verbs.
points: A phrasal verb is a verb followed by a particle (a small word such as up, out, into, on, off) that together have a new meaning.

Problem-solving phrasal verbs: figure out (understand or solve), work out (find the answer), come up with (think of an idea), look into (investigate), sort out (fix), carry on (continue), give up (stop trying).
Changing the particle changes the meaning: give up (stop trying), give in (accept defeat), give away (hand out for free).
More useful ones: put off (postpone), look after (take care of), run out of (have none left), find out (discover), turn down (refuse).

example.q: Think it through: Replace the words in brackets with a phrasal verb. 'Tara (thought of) a clever plan to save water in the school.'
steps: The phrasal verb for producing an idea is 'come up with'.
The sentence is in the past, so use 'came up with'.
example.answer: Tara came up with a clever plan to save water in the school.

learn.reallife: Everyday English is full of phrasal verbs: 'Switch off the fan', 'Pick up your bag', 'We ran out of sugar'.

items.q: Phrasal verb for 'think of an idea'

quiz.q: 'Don't give up, you are close to the answer!' Here 'give up' means ___.
quiz.explain: 'Give up' means to stop trying.
quiz.mistake: Reads the two words separately instead of as one phrasal verb

quiz.q: Choose the phrasal verb: Meera ___ a smart way to share the mangoes.
quiz.explain: 'Came up with' means thought of an idea. 'Came down with' means fell ill.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that the particle changes the meaning

quiz.q: Which phrasal verb means 'to investigate'?
quiz.explain: To look into something is to examine it carefully. 'Look up to' means to respect someone.
quiz.mistake: Picks any 'look' phrasal verb without checking the meaning

quiz.q: 'The school trip was put off because of the rain.' Here 'put off' means ___.
quiz.explain: 'Put off' means moved to a later time, which is postponed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'put off' means cancelled for good

quiz.q: Which sentence means 'We had no milk left'?
quiz.explain: To run out of something is to use it all up so none is left.
quiz.mistake: Picks another 'run' phrasal verb with a different meaning

quiz.q: 'Please look after my tulsi plant while I am away.' Here 'look after' means ___.
quiz.explain: To look after something is to take care of it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'after' here is about place or time

quiz.q: Which of these means 'to hand out for free'?
quiz.explain: 'Give away' means to give something for free. 'Give up' is stop trying; 'give in' is accept defeat.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that each particle gives a different meaning

quiz.q: A phrasal verb is made of ___.
options: a verb plus a particle such as up, out or into
a verb plus a suffix such as -ing
quiz.explain: Examples: give + up, look + into, run + out of. The words together carry a new meaning.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a phrasal verb is a verb with an ending added

teach.ask: Gappu blinks: 'Give up' and 'give away' both have 'give'. Why do they mean such different things?
teach.praise: Wow! A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, and that small word changes the whole meaning!
teach.nudge: What is added after 'give'? And does that small word change the meaning or keep it the same?
